Popular Safari extension StopTheMadness developer Jeff Johnson said the App Store rating fraud situation is "obvious" yet undetected by Apple, contradicting the company's claim that it reviews apps before listing them.

He noted that he wasn't actively looking for fraud on the App Store, but kept running into it, and cited the latest example...

The App Store as a 'safe and trusted place'

Apple has consistently pushed back against any antitrust measures involving third-party app stores or iPhone sideloading, only relenting when legally forced to. Even so, Apple continues to defend itself.

The company claims its motives aren't about money, but about protecting iPhone users from malware. Apple claimed last year, for example, that it blocked over $9 billion in fraudulent transactions.

However, multiple developers have questioned the App Store being a safe place, pointing to multiple scams involving millions of dollars. Just last month, three customers sued Apple after a fake wallet app emptied their Bitcoin holdings.

App Store rating fraud

App Store rating fraud has been a serious problem, with an earlier case involving a Chinese company running a factory-floor iPhone farm that downloaded apps and left five-star reviews.

StopTheMadness Safari extension developer Jeff Johnson pointed out the latest example of App Store rating fraud he has seen as "pervasive and obvious." He used TabControl Extension as his latest example.

He said that when he stumbled upon the app, it was ranked 12th among paid Safari extensions in the US Mac App Store, and used a screenshot that appeared to be AI-generated and fake.

Also worth noting is that the "4.9 out of 5" star rating in the fake screenshot misleadingly suggests this is the app's user rating on the App Store [...] Using App Store screenshots to make false statements is a common scam tactic I have mentioned in the past. When developers submit apps to the App Store, Apple reviews not only the app itself but also its listing materials and metadata, including screenshots. Yet the claims in these scam app screenshots are often blatantly absurd, and Apple approves them anyway [...] Apple claims its App Store protects users from dishonest developers. If the App Store's review process isn't working, what exactly are they doing? In reality, the App Store's review shouldn't require the kind of deep digging I do. A "4.9 out of 5" star rating in a screenshot should be a massive red flag. Apple has records of all ratings and reviews across every country, so they should know this is false advertising. I don't even need to download the app to determine the developer is trying to scam people.

As he pointed out, if a developer is trying to scam you out of your money from the start with their app, you certainly wouldn't trust them with your browsing data either.

9to5Mac's take

Of course, it's impossible to catch every single App Store scam, but fake ratings are so pervasive that this particular example should have been obvious to Apple, making it hard to understand how this extension passed review.

Apple should at the very least build a system that automatically triggers a stricter round of review when an app breaks into the top of any chart, re-examining the app and its claims.
